steps.title: Choose a collection by behaviour
steps.content: A list or array keeps an ordered sequence and often allows duplicates. A set stores unique values. A map or dictionary stores key-value pairs for lookup by key.
steps.example: Use a list for ordered marks, a set for unique roll numbers, and a map from roll number to student record.

steps.title: Remove duplicates
steps.prompt: Which collection is most directly suited to keeping only unique values?
steps.explanation: A set enforces uniqueness, so duplicate values are represented only once.

steps.title: Understand map lookup
steps.content: A map associates each key with a value. A hash map typically provides average O(1) lookup, insertion and deletion when keys are distributed well.
steps.example: student_by_id[1042] returns the record stored for ID 1042.

steps.title: Pick the right structure
steps.prompt: You need to count how many times each word appears. Which structure is a natural choice?
steps.explanation: A map can store each word as a key and its frequency as the value.

steps.title: Mutability and iteration
steps.content: Some collections are mutable, so their contents can change after creation. Iteration visits their elements. Avoid modifying a collection during iteration unless the language and algorithm explicitly support it.
steps.tip: Choose a collection based on ordering, uniqueness, lookup and update requirements.

questions.prompt: Which collection naturally removes duplicate values?

questions.explanation: A map or dictionary associates keys with values.

questions.prompt: Which structure preserves insertion order and allows duplicate entries in common languages?
questions.explanation: Lists represent ordered sequences and allow duplicates.

questions.prompt: What is average lookup time in a well-sized hash map?
questions.explanation: Expected hash-map lookup is O(1) with a good hash distribution.

questions.prompt: What is a common reason to use a set?
questions.explanation: Sets are useful for uniqueness tests and membership checks.
